title: Downtown Improvement District Stays in Place as Council Seeks Answers on Fees and Liens
excerpt: Laredo City Council decided not to dissolve the Central Laredo Municipal Management District, ordering a confidential survey of downtown property owners instead and requiring the district to report back by February on its fees, liens and foreclosure procedures.
content:
Laredo City Council has decided not to dissolve the downtown district that charges commercial property owners an added assessment for cleanup, safety and other improvements, according to the Laredo Morning Times.

After a discussion that ran nearly two hours, the council instead ordered a confidential survey of commercial property owners within the Central Laredo Municipal Management District, better known as the Downtown Business Improvement District. The district must return by February with information on its fees, liens and foreclosure procedures, and city management was directed to work with it on the concerns raised.

The Texas Legislature created the district in 2013 through Senate Bill 1601, authored by Sen. Judith Zaffirini and sponsored by Rep. Richard Raymond, giving it the power to levy taxes and assessments, charge fees and issue bonds. It sat largely dormant until the city and the district’s board began reactivating it in late 2024.

The district levied its first assessment in 2025, at 20 cents per $100 of assessed value on taxable commercial property, and began collecting in early 2026. Earlier city estimates put annual revenue at about $379,000.

Mayor Victor Treviño, who proposed the survey, said he supports downtown revitalization but has heard from owners who did not understand what the assessment pays for or what happens if they cannot pay. He raised questions about late charges, attorney fees, liens and foreclosure, and compared the setup to taxation without representation, since the council appoints the board from nominees approved through the district’s process while council members field owners’ complaints. He also said downtown vacancies have risen from about 33% to nearly 50% over the past couple of years.

Julian Rotnofsky, the district’s vice chairman, said owners and residents surveyed by the district ranked security, parking, economic development, lighting and cleaner streets among their top priorities. He said the board has adopted a voluntary four-year moratorium on foreclosures. If it is lifted, he said, a delinquent account would have to meet set thresholds, receive several notices and be offered a payment plan and hardship review before a two-thirds board vote could approve foreclosure. Rotnofsky could not immediately give specific late-fee or attorney-fee amounts or point to a single place where owners could find all of the rules.

District VII Council Member Vanessa Perez, who earlier this year pushed for written policies on repayment plans, late fees, liens and foreclosure, pressed for more clarity on the district’s rules and enforcement authority.

District III Council Member Melissa Cigarroa said the district was designed to pair private money from businesses with public investment downtown. She noted it has already started power washing and is planning landscaping and lighting work. “We need to give this business improvement district time to work,” she said.

District VIII Council Member Alyssa Cigarroa, whose district includes downtown, questioned dissolving a newly activated tool without an alternative plan. A representative of The Outlet Shoppes at Laredo, believed to be among the largest contributors to the assessment, also opposed dissolution, as did former city Planning and Zoning Director Orlando Navarro, who said ending the district would shift more of the cost of downtown improvements onto city taxpayers.

Police Chief Miguel Rodriguez told the council that officers have responded to thousands of calls and made more than 1,300 arrests downtown this year. He pointed to homelessness combined with drug use as a major challenge and discussed the need for more officers, community service officers and cleanup work.

The district describes its role as supplementing city services through power washing, graffiti removal, lighting, landscaping, security and economic development. Officials have also described it as a possible partner to the city’s Downtown Tax Increment Reinvestment Zone, which would focus on capital projects. For now, the 20-cent assessment remains in effect.

Sources: Laredo Morning Times, Nov. 27, 2026; Local National, Nov. 27, 2026.
